title: Weakly Nonlinear Dynamics of Unstable Modes in Jammed Amorphous Solids
authors: Kota Noto, Harukuni Ikeda, Kuniyasu Saitoh, Hisao Hayakawa
abstract: We investigate the structural evolution in jammed amorphous solids by analyzing the eigenmodes of a generalized Hessian matrix that incorporates spatial modulation via wave numbers. Unlike the conventional Hessian, this generalized formulation captures linearly unstable modes through a Fourier-based extension of the Hessian matrix, enabling us to study responses beyond the mechanically stable regime. We demonstrate that the excitation of unstable eigenmodes leads to structural rearrangements independent of the initial perturbation by the simulation. Furthermore, we derive a weakly nonlinear amplitude equation to describe the growth and saturation of these unstable modes, analogous to the Landau equation. Our framework provides a pathway to understand instability-driven configuration changes in disordered solids.
summary: This work analyzes structural instabilities in jammed amorphous solids by extending standard Hessian analysis using wave numbers. By developing a weakly nonlinear amplitude equation, the authors provide a theoretical framework to model how these unstable modes drive large-scale structural rearrangements beyond simple mechanical stability limits.
main_problem: The study investigates how structural evolution occurs in jammed amorphous solids by analyzing eigenmodes that become linearly unstable beyond the mechanically stable regime.
main_result: The authors derived a weakly nonlinear amplitude equation, analogous to the Landau equation, to describe the growth and subsequent saturation of these structurally destabilizing modes.
method: The approach combines linear stability analysis using a generalized Hessian matrix (extended via Fourier transforms) with the development of weak nonlinearity theory.
model_or_system: The system modeled is jammed amorphous solids composed of repulsive particles, governed by overdamped dynamics derived from a pairwise potential energy function. The analysis uses mesoscopic periodic-cell constructions to incorporate spatial modulation via wave numbers (k).
key_observables: Eigenvalues of the generalized Hessian matrix ($\lambda_n(k)$), which determine stability; and the nonlinear coefficient ($\chi_E$) used in amplitude equations.
important_parameters: The analysis is sensitive to specific parameter regimes, such as $	ext{PL}^4/(\kappa d_s^4) \sim O(1)$, and compares results across different system sizes ($N=32$ vs $N=512$).
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include using a quasi-periodic cell structure (Bloch-like approximation) to characterize long-wavelength modulations, which is an idealization for amorphous solids.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate eigenvalue branches showing where modes become negative (unstable), demonstrate mode hybridization between different character types at finite k, and compare system-size dependence of stability metrics against theoretical lines.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the dynamics via a potential energy function to linearizing around equilibrium using a generalized Hessian. It then applies Fourier transforms to analyze wave-vector dependent instabilities before deriving the final weakly nonlinear amplitude equation for mode evolution.
why_interesting: While focused on classical disordered solids, the mathematical framework of analyzing instability growth via Landau-like equations and spectral analysis is highly relevant to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body quantum systems near phase transitions or critical points.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 An example of a tile structure consisting of a 3×3 array of cells. Each cell consists of a packing of 32 particles.

Fig. 2 The four lowest eigenvalue branches along the kxex-direction (blue) and the kyey-direction (green) for P/κ = 5 × 10−4 and N = 128. All branches are non-negative in (a), whereas the lowest branch becomes negative near the X point in (b). The labeled points (A)–(G) in panel (b) indicate the wave numbers at which the corresponding eigenvectors are shown in Fig. 3 as panels (a)–(g), respectively.

Fig. 3 Eigenvectors corresponding to the labeled points (A)–(G) in Fig. 2(b), shown here as panels (a)–(g), respectively. Panels (a)–(d) show the eigenvectors of the lowest branch in the kxex direction at wave numbers (a) kx = 0, (b) kx = 9π/20L, (c) kx = 11π/20L, and (d) kx = π/L, respectively. Panels (e) and (f) depict the eigenmodes corresponding to the third-lowest and fourth-lowest branches at k = 0, i.e., the lowest nonzero eigenmode and the second-lowest nonzero eigenmode. Panel (g) shows the eigenvector of the lowest branch in the kyey direction at ky = π/L.

Fig. 4 Displacements of grains after adding the perturbation along the direction of the eigenvector for the case with a positive eigenvalue, where red arrows in (a) indicate the initial perturbative displacements of grains and blue arrows in (b) exhibit the final displacements of grains after the relaxation. These figures demonstrate the stability of the initial configuration against the perturbation.

Fig. 5 Displacements of grains after adding the perturbation along the direction of the eigenvector for the case with a negative eigenvalue, where red arrows in (a) indicate the initial perturbative displacements of grains and blue arrows in (b) exhibit the final displacements of grains after the relaxation. These figures demonstrate the instability of the initial configuration against the perturbation.
